title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the sound, the route and the letter

questions.prompt: Four words of the module are being sorted into sound boxes. Match each one with the key word whose vowel it shares.
questions.explanation: through has no oo in it at all and still belongs in the long box of moon, beside food, blue, routine and lagoon. mouth goes in the wide box of now, with found, south, around and countryside. wood takes the short vowel of book. flood ends in the same three letters as wood and sits two boxes away, on the plain vowel of bus. Two traps are hidden in the four: the same letters give different sounds, since wood and flood share -ood and part company, and different letters give the same sound, since through and food have no spelling in common and land together. Sort by the key word you can hear, never by the letters you can see.

questions.prompt: Two notices are pinned at the entrance to a nature park: "Keep to the path along the river" and "Do not walk off the marked path". Taken together, what do they ask visitors to do?

options.text: Cross the river, and never leave the marked way.
Cross the river, and walk beside the marked way.
Follow the river bank, and begin walking where the marked way ends.
Follow the river bank, and never leave the marked way.

questions.explanation: along the river means following the line of the river, so the visitor keeps the bank beside her, and walk off the path means leaving the surface you were on, so the second notice forbids leaving it: "Follow the river bank, and never leave the marked way." "Cross the river, and never leave the marked way." reads along as across, which would send the walker over the water and away from the bank. "Follow the river bank, and begin walking where the marked way ends." reads off as the off of set off, a departure, whereas here it is the opposite of on. "Cross the river, and walk beside the marked way." misreads both notices at once, and beside the way is precisely where the second notice forbids you to be.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The ferry did not sail ___ a strike at the port."
questions.explanation: What follows the gap is a noun group, a strike at the port, with no verb of its own, so the gap can only take a preposition; and the strike is the cause of the cancellation, which gives "owing to". "as" does introduce a cause, but it is a conjunction and needs a whole clause after it, as in as there was a strike at the port. "although" is a conjunction too, so it fails on the same count, and it announces a contrast rather than a cause. "so that" is a conjunction that announces a purpose, which would make the strike the aim of the cancellation instead of its reason.

questions.prompt: A traveller writing a letter of complaint has finished describing everything that went wrong during her week. If her letter follows the three-part plan, what does she write next?

options.text: A polite request for the company's latest brochure.
A second, longer description of the noise from the building site.
The exact dates of the holiday and the name of the resort.
What she expects the company to do about it.

questions.explanation: The plan runs reason for writing, then details of the problems, then what is expected from the company, so once the problems are told the third part is due: "What she expects the company to do about it." "The exact dates of the holiday and the name of the resort." belongs to the first part and should already be at the top of the letter. "A second, longer description of the noise from the building site." reopens the second part, and repeating a complaint at length weakens it instead of adding anything. "A polite request for the company's latest brochure." asks for something that has nothing to do with the spoilt week and would make the whole letter look pointless.

questions.prompt: A traveller stepped off the coach and, in the same movement, the guide handed her a key. Which sentence reports the two actions the way English usually does?

options.text: When the traveller stepped off the coach, the guide handed her a key.
When the traveller stepped off the coach, the guide had handed her a key.
When the traveller had stepped off the coach, the guide handed her a key.
When the traveller had stepped off the coach, the guide had handed her a key.

questions.explanation: When two past actions are close in time, or closely connected, the past perfect is not usually used, and two simple pasts are enough: "When the traveller stepped off the coach, the guide handed her a key." Nobody could get that order wrong, so marking it adds weight and no meaning. "When the traveller had stepped off the coach, the guide handed her a key." is the over-marked version: it is not broken English, but it opens a gap between two moments that belong together. "When the traveller stepped off the coach, the guide had handed her a key." puts the past perfect on the other half and claims the key changed hands before she was off the coach. "When the traveller had stepped off the coach, the guide had handed her a key." pushes both actions before some third moment that the sentence never names.

questions.prompt: Complete the last line of a letter of complaint: "I hope you will look into this, and I look forward ___ from you before the end of the month."
questions.explanation: In look forward to, the to is a preposition and not the to of an infinitive, so the verb that follows it takes the -ing form: "to hearing" from you. "to hear" is the trap the expression is famous for, because the eye reads to and expects an infinitive. "hearing" has the right form but drops the preposition that belongs to the expression, and look forward on its own is not English. "for hearing" keeps an -ing form but swaps the preposition, and look forward for does not exist.
